exam: What bedside test distinguishes compressive from ischemic CN III palsy? — Check pupillary reaction; a dilated, non‑reactive pupil suggests compression.
A 55‑year‑old diabetic presents with ptosis and down‑and‑out eye but normal pupils. What is the most likely cause? — Microvascular ischaemia of the oculomotor nerve.

How would you manage a patient with pupil‑involving palsy in a hospital without CT? — Arrange urgent transfer, start steroids only if meningitis suspected, and monitor for worsening neurological signs.
Why should anticholinergic eye drops be avoided in CN III palsy? — They can further dilate the pupil and mask progression of a compressive lesion.
What systemic conditions common in East Africa increase risk of microvascular CN III palsy? — Uncontrolled diabetes, hypertension, sickle‑cell disease, and HIV‑associated vasculopathy.

Describe the ‘cover‑uncover’ test and its relevance in CN III palsy. — The patient covers each eye in turn; diplopia that resolves when the affected eye is covered indicates the palsied eye is causing the misalignment.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt immediate neurosurgical referral? — Sudden severe headache or thunderclap headache with new CN III palsy.
How does TB meningitis cause a third nerve palsy? — Inflammation and basal exudates compress the nerve at the midbrain‑cisternal junction.
ai.title: Third Cranial Nerve Palsy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A third nerve palsy causes diplopia, ptosis and abnormal eye movements due to impairment of oculomotor function. Recognise patterns, identify urgent causes, and manage in low‑resource settings.

b: Diplopia worsens on looking toward the affected side
Eyelid droop (ptosis) due to levator weakness
Pupil may be dilated (parasympathetic involvement) or spared (ischemic cause)
sections.p: The oculomotor nerve supplies most extra‑ocular muscles, levator palpebrae, and parasympathetic fibres to the pupil. Palsy produces down‑and‑out gaze, ptosis, and variable pupil dilation.

b: Pupil‑involving palsy → compressive lesion, urgent imaging
Pupil‑sparing palsy → microvascular disease, often diabetic or hypertensive
Assess for associated signs: headache, altered consciousness, visual field loss
sections.p: Distinguish compressive (e.g., aneurysm, tumour) from ischemic (microvascular) aetiologies. Pupil involvement is the classic bedside discriminator.

b: Rapid identification of pupil‑involving palsy triggers referral for CT/MRA
Blood glucose, blood pressure, and HIV status guide aetiology in the tropics
Uncontrolled hypertension, sickle‑cell disease, and TB meningitis can precipitate ischemic palsy
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, many patients present with diabetes‑related microvascular palsy, but aneurysmal rupture remains a fatal emergency that may be missed without imaging.
